method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

worlds.line: Your refill's ready, it's behind the counter now.
worlds.reply: Great, I'll take it now, I've got my card out.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line reports that the medicine has already been dispensed and is waiting to be handed over. The reply that takes it straight away and reaches for a card is the cooperative next move. The reply asking whether another branch has stock treats the medicine as unavailable; the reply promising to ring the clinic treats prescriber approval as still outstanding; the reply choosing the cheaper generic answers a choice that was never offered.

kills.1: The line says the refill is "behind the counter", so the reply that goes hunting for another branch with stock is looking for something that is already here.
kills.2: Since "Your refill's ready", the reply that promises to call the clinic and chase an approval is chasing a step that has already been completed.
kills.3: The line only reports that the "refill's ready"; the reply that picks the generic over the brand answers a question the pharmacist never asked.

worlds.line: We're out of stock, the supplier can't send more this week.
worlds.reply: Is there another branch nearby that might have some?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line reports a supply failure with no fix available at this counter. Asking whether a nearby branch holds any is the natural way to keep the errand alive. The reply that takes the medicine now assumes there is something to hand over; the reply that promises to ring the clinic blames the prescriber rather than the supply chain; the reply choosing the generic assumes two versions are sitting on the shelf.

kills.0: The pharmacist says "We're out of stock", so the reply that takes the medicine now and produces a card is collecting something that is not there.
kills.2: The obstacle named is that "the supplier can't send more", so the reply that undertakes to call the clinic for approval is fixing the wrong problem.
kills.3: With the shelf "out of stock", the reply that opts for the generic over the brand chooses between two things that are equally unavailable.

worlds.reply: I'll call the clinic this afternoon and ask them.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line states a procedural precondition that the customer, not the pharmacist, is placed to clear. Undertaking to ring the clinic that afternoon addresses exactly that precondition. The reply that collects the medicine now assumes it has been dispensed; the reply hunting for another branch assumes a stock problem; the reply picking the generic assumes a choice of versions was on the table.

kills.1: Nothing was said about supply, only that "The doctor has to approve" it, so the reply that shops the prescription round other branches misreads the hold-up.
kills.3: Since "The doctor has to approve" it first, the reply that settles on the generic is choosing a version before anything can be dispensed at all.

The reply that takes the medicine now skips past a question still open; the reply asking about other branches assumes a shortage the question denies; the reply promising to ring the clinic assumes an approval problem nobody raised.

kills.2: The counter is asking about "the generic version", not about paperwork, so the reply that promises to call the clinic for approval invents a hold-up.
